review:
Hearthlands, developed and published by Four White Cats, is a city-building and management game that leans heavily on classic design sensibilities while introducing a more relaxed, simulation-driven approach to governing a medieval-fantasy settlement. It doesn’t chase the complexity or spectacle of modern strategy titles; instead, it focuses on creating a living system where your role is less about issuing constant commands and more about shaping the conditions in which your town can grow. This shift in perspective gives the game a distinct rhythm, one that prioritizes observation and planning over micromanagement.

At its foundation, Hearthlands is about building a functioning settlement from the ground up. You establish resource chains, construct homes and production buildings, and ensure that your population has access to food, work, and basic services. What sets it apart is the way these systems operate. Citizens are not directly controlled; they make their own decisions based on available resources and their assigned roles. This creates a sense of autonomy within the simulation, where the town evolves in response to the structures you put in place rather than through constant player intervention. It can be rewarding to see systems align and operate smoothly, though it also introduces moments of unpredictability when things don’t behave as expected.

Managing the balance between growth and stability forms the core gameplay loop. Expanding too quickly can strain resources, while growing too slowly can leave your settlement vulnerable or stagnant. Production chains must be carefully maintained, and the flow of goods needs to remain consistent to support both the population and further development. At the same time, external pressures such as hostile creatures or rival factions require attention, adding a layer of tension that prevents the experience from becoming entirely passive. Diplomacy and trade offer alternative ways to interact with the world, giving players additional tools to support their settlement’s survival.

The game’s sandbox nature is one of its defining strengths. There is no rigid path to follow, allowing players to shape their settlement according to their own priorities. Whether focusing on economic growth, defensive strength, or a balanced approach, the game supports a variety of playstyles. This flexibility encourages experimentation and gives each playthrough a slightly different feel, especially when combined with procedurally generated maps. However, because the game lacks a strong narrative or structured progression, much of the motivation comes from the player’s own goals, which may not appeal to everyone.

Visually, Hearthlands adopts a straightforward isometric style that emphasizes clarity over detail. Buildings, units, and resources are easy to identify, which helps when managing multiple systems at once, but the overall presentation is relatively simple. There is a certain charm in watching the town gradually take shape, though the visuals do not evolve significantly as the game progresses. The audio design follows a similar pattern, providing a subtle backdrop that supports the experience without drawing attention to itself.

Where the game begins to show its limitations is in the depth of its systems. While the mechanics are interconnected, they are not particularly complex, and once the player understands how to maintain a stable settlement, the challenge begins to diminish. Over time, the gameplay loop can feel repetitive, with fewer new elements introduced to keep things fresh. The indirect control system, while interesting, can also lead to frustration, particularly when citizens make inefficient decisions that disrupt carefully planned systems.

Despite these shortcomings, Hearthlands succeeds in offering a calm and approachable management experience. Its slower pace and emphasis on system design make it well-suited for players who enjoy watching a settlement grow organically rather than constantly directing every action. It captures the feel of older city-building games while simplifying some of their more demanding aspects, resulting in a game that is easy to engage with even if it lacks long-term depth.

In the end, Hearthlands is a solid and quietly enjoyable entry in the city-building genre. It doesn’t aim to be expansive or highly detailed, but it delivers a focused experience that highlights the satisfaction of creating and maintaining a functioning system. For players who appreciate a more relaxed, sandbox-oriented approach to management games, it offers a worthwhile experience, even if it doesn’t stand out as a deeply complex or highly polished title.

I grew up on Caesar III. Right there with Red Alert 1, Tiberian Sun, Lionel's, and Rollercoaster Tycoon all the way through to Factorio, Rimworld, and They Are Billions. I'm always searching for another great game that can fit in that city builder-management game and yet here I am shocked that I did not hear about this game until now. Without a doubt, this is an exceptionally well done and finished Impression Games-like game with an Anno-like heavy emphasis on resource provision to tiered residents except instead of sailing or flying your resources to and fro you do it through a classic early 2000s city builder with good manually drawn graphics to boot rather than the bloom-infested 3D eyesores (Banished).

The current Steam market is finally filling up with new city builder games and I've been buying and trying many of them out and if you've done the same, then you probably already know, but 1-in-2 of these new city builders are engaging in an effective demonstration of the idea that they're doing you a favor by letting you in on their Early Access limbo hell and yet none of them are even half the game this is - and it's not even in Early Access, it's already out since 2017. A finished city builder game, ready to enjoy in full, RIGHT NOW. I can't believe it.

Perfect amalgamation of the classic Impression Games city builder game loop (improved by a few modern quality of life changes) and nostalgic aesthetics from Northland, as well as elements from 1st generation RTS games such as Tzar, where the RPG influence was still fresh and strong, and you had magical artifacts, swords and chests full of coins scattered throughout the map for your soldiers to pick up.

I LOVE some of the little ideas such as the unemployment-vs-taxation mechanic, I'm genuinely learning useful stuff that I'm gonna have to keep in mind for my own game development, and I wish more games did.

Honestly the only possible complaints I could think of are:
- I wish I could save & load specific savefiles from the pause menu
- The settings could be better (e.g. edge scroll, mouse sensitivity, keybinds, ability to disable window always in front etc.)
- The combat could be a bit more polished (unit commands sometimes are ignored, there's no drag selection, etc.)
- The music becomes a smidgen repetitive after a while, and some of the sounds get quite annoying (like the winery pumps)
- The UI could be a bit more polished, it's useable but clunky at times, and the undo button from the Impression Games titles is dearly missed
- The raiding RNG should definitely be rebalanced (you pretty much are required to max your entire forces, wait for the city to attack you, and attack back multiple times in a row in order to eventually defeat them - even though the inspector says "we are very likely to win this battle")

That being said, overall a fantastic city builder. 100% recommend.

Hearthlands is a city planner clone of Caesar 3, Pharaoh and the various games from the City Builder series of Sierra. In Hearthlands you play one of four different cultures who differ by the basic resources they can produce and by one specialized military unit.

The game's presentation is average. Graphics, UI and controls all work well enough to be able to manage the build in a slow pace. The game's pace is the first problem you may encounter. You can speed up progression in Hearthlands by twice to 3 times as fast, but it usually means you'll get production issues to show up just as fast. The updates on the resource status pane don't reflect how bad your situation can be. For instance you can have a deficiency in medicine lasting several years without any issues rising. Have a deficiency in logs however and that can lead to a catastrophe. Resources are not well categorized enough to understand this while playing the game.

Resource balance is flimsy at best. You need so many log cabins in this game, I've started recognizing situations as "Plank Apocalypse" or "Log Addiction". Having 20-30 cabins for any size-able city is normal. Wood is essential to about everything. The same can not be said of fringe resources like Eggs. If you want to accumulate those, same problem, but worst, the production is actually useless unless you need feathers. Multiple food resources suffer from starvation, because their values are engineered to be much lower.

With 3000 population, you can go about with 2 bakeries, and only 1 mill, but you'll need more than 12 log cabins, 10 grain farms, 10 furniture shops, etc.. It doesn't really make any sense as on another game I needed a lot more of everything. Eventually the map just crawls because of the amount of buildings required for production. You can't upgrade individual structures. The crawling obviously affects balance as you'll suddenly end up in "Plank Apocalypse" just for producing 8 spears. Military units can cost a lot if you make specialize units and I swear some times the upkeep is 10 times what it's supposed to be. 

Some other issues show up when harvesters pick the resource the further away from their farm. It seems the algorithm scans from the corners of their range. That means they'll frequently visit other farms and harvest resources they shouldn't be harvesting. Starvation issues happen between storage houses if they're on the same roads with the same resource specs. The game is not very intelligent when it auto-manages for you and unfortunately it feels broken very often.

Campaigns are only about answering step goals in a sequential manner which you can reach whenever it suits you. Even mobs attacking your cities on the map are triggered on cue. Either population increase or global net worth of your buildings, it's easy to reload a save game and make sure you can fence a group of spiders before it does any damage.

Overall Hearthlands is boring with very little challenge. There are no guides or wikis to help players figure out the mechanics. You'll have to put up with the hostility of the developer and send him private emails. Unfortunately this game feels like reinventing the square wheel with too many consistency issues to me. Pick it up  on sale if you must, but there are better city planners out there.

As we all know, the city building genre is not doing that well right now. Sure, there's still quite a lot of such games around and some of them even come with pretty interesting mechanics, but still, there's a big problem with them. Even though city building games started as some sort of sandboxes in titles like [b]Don Daglow[/b]'s [b]Utopia[/b], [b]Will Wright[/b]'s [b]SimCity[/b] and [b]Impressions Games[/b]' [b]Caesar[/b] (which added a proper military that was only hinted in [b]Utopia[/b]), the genre eventually evolved into something way cooler. I'm talking, of course, about the campaign mode. Not only it was a great way to learn the basics step-by-step, it was also really interesting to play through. Just because, aside from our usual endless thing, we've got ourselves a series of missions with different goals in them.

Thanks to that, the city building fun got on the whole new level. We've got ourselves juicy gang wars in [b]Mob Rule[/b] (sequel to [b]Constructor[/b], which didn't have proper campaign in it), we've got humorous fantasy tale in [b]Beasts & Bumpkins[/b], we've got [b]Settlers[/b] with all of its variants and, of course, we've got [b]Impressions Games[/b]' [b]Caesar III[/b], [b]Pharaoh[/b], [b]Zeus[/b] and [b]Emperor[/b]. Those four marked the highest point for city building genre. Unfortunately, soon after that... things started to go backward. Instead of evolving, city building games started to go back to the basics. And as the result, we started to get things like [b]Banished[/b]. Which were still pretty cute, but... you know. Playing them felt like returning to [b]80[/b]s. And not in a way you may want to. Like I said, even though modern games often offer us some interesting elements (like [b]Dawn of Man[/b] for example), having a sandbox mode as the main dish makes them feel way too archaic for my liking. Seriously, guys. Look at the calendar. You can't just offer us the core mechanics and call it a day. We need more content. We need missions!

So... here comes that Russian guy [b]Sergey Pershakov[/b]. And yes, as long as we won't count [b]Alexey Lyukshin[/b] who worked on visuals and two other guys ([b]Sergey Fyodorov[/b] and [b]Seth Cruse[/b]) who helped with the music, [b]Hearthlands[/b] was made by only one guy. Doesn't sound promising, huh? Well, it sure doesn't. And let me tell you – when you'll start this game for the first time? You'll be like “[i]FFFFFFUUUUUUUU...[/i]” For many reasons. First (and most importantly)... well, look at screenshots. What does this game look like? I'll tell you what it looks like – it looks like a bloody mobile game. And you know what? There's a good reason for that since [b]Hearthlands[/b] is... well, it's a [b]JAVA[/b] app, OK? Yes, you heard that right. It's a freakin' [b]JAVA[/b] game. Bet you didn't expect to hear that nowadays, huh? Things like [b]JAVA[/b] and [b]Flash[/b] games are something long forgotten at this point. And yet, here... we... are. A [b]JAVA[/b] game that asks for likes and reposts right on its title screen. Joy... But. Yes, there's a “but” in all that. Because... believe it or not, this game is actually pretty nice. [i]Surprisingly[/i] nice.

Believe it or not, that one guy got things right and offered us exactly what we've been waiting for. An old school experience with both sandbox and a proper campaign. Campaign that does things totally right. Not only we've got ourselves proper goals, every mission in this game has not one, but many different goals that'll unlock one after another.  There are [b]12[/b] missions here that vary from easy to hard and, like I said, every mission has a few steps you'll need to go through in order to win. Unfortunately, there's no proper story, but then again, cit building games with the story are pretty rare, while missions are actually pretty interesting, so... yeah. It'll totally do.

And as for the core mechanics? Everything is pretty neat too. Naturally, [b]Hearthlands[/b] is based mostly on [b]Impressions Games[/b]' titles, but it actually adds some things from the other famous titles to the formula. So, it's not just a clone. [b]Hearthlands[/b] feels like somebody desperately tried to make city building game for themselves. For their own personal preferences. It takes pretty much everything that used to make such games cool back in the days and calls it a day. You can also notice that in the [b]UI[/b] and micromanagement. The only thing I totally disliked is how the building panel's placed, but aside from that? Everything here is comfortable and easy to understand / use. Sure, this game doesn't offer any special depth. It's just our standard stuff. We build and upgrade houses to increase population (hello, [b]Caesar[/b]), we produce resources (like in [b]Settlers[/b] series, different nations have different approach here), we trade and / or fight with our neighbors and so on. But what's really cool here is that the game offers you the exact info / micromanagement you need in the exact places you want them. You're playing the game and then you're like “[i]It'll be really cool to get more details about the production if I'll click on that building[/i]”. And guess what? The detailed info sits right there. Same thing with the micromanagement. There's exactly as much as casual player would want and it feels both logical and comfortable. Feels really, [i]really[/i] good. I can't say that [b]Hearthlands[/b] is a perfect game to start for those who never played such things before (it may be a little bit more tricky than it looks and it does require some learning before you'll start having a real fun with it), but still, if you're ready to invest some time in it and learn? It's pretty rewarding.

Unfortunately, there's one thing to heavily ruin the final impression. And that thing is... balance. Obviously. Pretty much everybody who played this game on its early stages complained about it and even though [b]Mr. Pershakov[/b] sure listened and fixed some things, this game is still unbalanced as heck. I'm not sure if it's actually possible for a single man to provide us with properly polished experience and [b]Sergey[/b] sure deserves a lot of credit for what he achieved here, but the fact stays – you're looking for perfectly balanced city building game? Look somewhere else. You won't find it here. You probably won't notice it at the beginning (especially if you'll start with the campaign, in which many different things, like magic spells for example, are locked until later), but the more you'll play – the more you'll get “[i]Wait, why?[/i]” effect. Sure, I can't say that this game is broken or something. Far from it. I'm just trying to say that those who know their city building stuff, may have some unpleasant balance surprises on the way.

And yet, [b]Hearthlands[/b] turned out to be a nice surprise for me. I can't say I'll want to return to it often in the future, but honestly, this is how I like my city building games. It's like me and [b]Mr. Pershakov[/b] feel [i]exactly[/i] the same about city building genre. This right here is exactly what I wanted. And even though [b]Hearthlands[/b] is not balanced enough and comes with that certain cheap aftertaste of the mobile game (no, seriously, [b]JAVA[/b]?), I had more fun with it than I had with more ambitious titles lately. If you still haven't played classic titles from the past, some of which I've mentioned above, you should totally go for them first. Just because... you know. This game here feels more like a basic nod to the good old times than a real attempt to create a proper new name in the genre. But if you've already played and finished both well-known titles like [b]Caesar[/b] and less-known gems like [b]Beasts & Bumpkins[/b], then [b]Hearthlands[/b] can give you quite some good time, really. Just make sure you know what you're dealing with here. Dixi.

[i]Hearthlands[/i] est un city-builder méconnu qui rappellera des souvenirs aux adeptes des jeux Sierra ([i]Caesar III[/i], [i]Pharaon[/i], [i]Zeus[/i], etc.). Il propose une campagne de 12 missions qui vous tiendra en haleine une trentaine d'heures, ce qui est assez honnête : cette durée de vie pourra être nettement revue à la hausse si vous visez le 100%, notamment à cause de plusieurs succès plutôt longs et pénibles à obtenir. Cependant, la difficulté reste faible (faillite impossible, constructions autorisées même si vous êtes financièrement dans le rouge, etc.) et peut laisser penser que ce jeu est trop simple, voire simpliste. 

Malgré cela, on passe un agréable moment à gérer et voir grandir sa ville. Il faut tout de même signaler que la gestion militaire des unités sur le terrain est laborieuse et pas du tout intuitive, mais cela n'a pas gâché mon expérience globale sur ce jeu.

En conclusion, je recommande surtout ce titre aux nostalgiques des jeux de gestion à l'ancienne car tout autre public risquerait de trouver [i]Hearthlands[/i] fade et insipide.

Jeux de gestion de ressources à la Pharao / Caesar / Zeus. Un poil perdu au début pour la prise en main, il se maîtrise progressivement grâce à la campagne qui propose une très bonne durée de vie. 
Graphisme et ambiance très sympathique. Sa simplicité est son point fort

Un jeu de gestion de cité dans un univers médiéval fantastique fort intéressant et prenant qui selon moi n'a rien à envier aux ténors du genre. 

La campagne est sympa et permet de se familiariser avec les nombreuses fonctionnalités. Chaque peuple étant différent, leur gestion économique et militaire diffère également donc les parties se suivent mais ne se ressemblent pas.

Hearthlands est bien pensé et très mignon visuellement. Pas besoin d'un pc à 2000 boules pour le faire tourner, et ça c'est cool. 

La gestion économique est complète, aux petits oignons et logique. Logique dans le sens où on ne vous demandera pas des bottes, une chaise, une paire de ciseaux, un buffet à vaisselle, de l'or et un sac de farine pour faire du... jambon! 

La gestion militaire est simple d'accès (ce qui n'est pas le cas de tous les jeux de gestion...). Lorsqu'un voisin vous ennuie par exemple, vous avez la possibilité d'ouvrir la carte globale et d'envoyer à l'assaut les troupes que vous aurez sélectionné afin de faire taire ce vile faquin et d'en faire, en cas de victoire, votre vassal. Mais vous aurez également du "ménage" à faire sur la carte principale, pour protéger votre cité des vilaines engeances. Les combats sont plaisants et vos troupes gagnent des points d'xp donc, des niveaux. Cool!  
 
La partie commerce n'est pas pénible non plus (ouf!). Et ça tombe bien car chaque peuple manquera d'une ou plusieurs ressources donc il vous faudra obligatoirement vendre votre surplus et acheter les produits manquants. Commercialement parlant, il n'est pas toujours évident de trouver le bon équilibre, mais... C'est tout l'art d'un jeu de gestion.

Hearthlands ne se laisse pas dompter facilement, il ne s'agit pas d'un jeu "casu". Va falloir réfléchir un pitit peu quand même et passer quelques heures en jeu pour maîtriser toutes les subtilités de ce titre. 
Mais Hearthlands n'est pas punitif au point d'être frustrant car il vous est permis de corriger une ou plusieurs erreurs de gestion en pleine partie avant la terrible banqueroute. 
Il m'est arrivé de recommencer une ou deux parties mais franchement j'avais fait n'importe quoi. Oui bon bah c'était au début quoi! :)

Après 30 heures de jeu, je n'en suis qu'à la moitié de la campagne (oui je prends mon temps), et je passe vraiment de bons moments en compagnie de ce hearthlands. Il me rappelle les anciens Settlers et Anno.

Il est traduit en langue française, et même si par moment cette traduction est approximative, elle a le mérite d'exister. 
Aucun bug à signaler. D'ailleurs, si les devs ne sont que deux, je leur tire mon chapeau car Hearthlands est bien codé, c'est du beau boulot!

Une réclamation peut-être? Mais oui tout à fait : Un peu plus d'options disponibles dans le menu au niveau des paramètres du jeu et un peu plus de choix dans les musiques parce que le tour est vite fait. 

En conclusion, hearthlands est une bonne découverte en plus d'être très abordable en soldes. 
Je recommande! 
Aussi bien pour ceux qui aimeraient découvrir le genre que pour les joueurs expérimentés en mal de jeux de gestion.

The bones of a great classic city builder are in place. It has a lot of potential. I'd just like to see it fleshed out a bit more. Overall I had a great time. 

Feedback time!

First, I'd like to see some more efforts at in-game documentation (tool-tip, in-game-wiki.) The majority of my time was spent trying to figure out the volume of demand for the houses and I still don't think I have that nailed down. While I enjoy a puzzle, I kinda feel like it shouldn't be that much of a mystery how much furniture to supply. 

Second, it is a little slim on progression. The research system is a nice start but none of it particularily felt different in the same way progressing through the ages of Empire Earth would, for example. Perhaps Hearthlands knows what it is and purposefull foregoes more complex progression. Good mechanics, well balanced trump everything anyway. 

If you have a hankering for a classic city-builder than you can play on a lazy Sunday, this is the game for you!
